title: Mapping How Proteins Sit in Membranes
endLine: Washes test burial; protease with and without detergent proves each side.

scenes.tts: How deeply does a protein sit in a membrane, and which way does it face? Some proteins cling to one surface. Others pierce the oily core, with ends on opposite sides. Watching an intact membrane cannot tell them apart. Two paired assays test burial and sidedness.

scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section of a closed lipid bilayer vesicle in buffer, cytosol outside and teal lumen inside, drifting gently. Before narration names them, two unmarked proteins settle on the bilayer: one perched on the outer face, one spanning the core with question marks on both ends. As the opening question is spoken, the question marks pulse; this vesicle stays in place as the film's carried world.
The carried vesicle dims gently behind bold high-contrast title text: 'Mapping How Proteins Sit in Membranes', then the title fades out.

scenes.tts: First, test burial. Wash membranes with high salt, or with high p H, called alkaline extraction. Salt and high p H loosen proteins held only by contacts at the membrane's face. Surface-clinging peripheral proteins come off into the liquid. Core-buried integral proteins stay behind when membranes are spun down into a pellet. Only soap-like detergent, which dissolves the bilayer, releases them.

scenes.visual: Schematic. Across the same vesicle membrane, a high-salt and high-pH wash sweeps through. The surface-clinging peripheral protein detaches and drifts off into the liquid while the core-spanning integral protein remains embedded in the spun-down membrane pellet. Next, soap-like detergent rings surround and dissolve the bilayer into micelles, freeing the integral protein.

scenes.tts: Once a protein stays in the core, ask its topology: which end faces each side? Break cells, and E R membranes reseal into sealed microsomes with their lumen inside. Put distinct antibody tags on both ends, then add protein-cutting protease outside. Protease cannot cross a sealed bilayer. It removes the cytosolic tag, leaving the lumenal tag intact.

scenes.visual: Schematic. The bilayer reforms as the sealed ER microsome (teal lumen inside, cytosol outside) carrying one spanning protein with a gold tag outside and a cyan tag inside. Protease scissor icons drift in the outer buffer, bounce off the intact membrane, and clip away the outer gold tag while the inner cyan tag stays intact. On a schematic gel strip beside the vesicle, the gold band vanishes and the cyan band remains.

scenes.tts: Pause and test that conclusion. Suppose one tag survives protease treatment on your gel. Does survival alone prove that tag sat inside the lumen? What else could protect it, and what control rules that out?

scenes.visual: Schematic. The sealed microsome and schematic gel strip stay on screen while a high-contrast question card appears above: 'Does surviving protease prove a tag is lumenal? What control rules out another cause?' The surviving inner cyan tag pulses beside a question mark.
Thinking pause: the question card, sealed microsome, and schematic gel strip stay steady on screen with a slow ambient glow on the question mark.

scenes.tts: No: the tag itself might resist the protease. Add detergent first to open the vesicles. If both tags vanish, the sealed membrane did the protecting. Washes test burial, while protease with and without detergent proves each side. One extraction catch: lipid-anchored proteins can also resist washes, since their lipid tail sits in the bilayer.

scenes.visual: Schematic. Detergent opens the sealed microsome; protease scissors now enter and digest the inner cyan tag too, erasing the cyan band on the schematic gel strip. Next, on the restored bilayer, a lipid-anchored protein tethered by a lipid tail dipped into the bilayer resists a high-salt and high-pH wash, highlighting why washes alone may not separate it from an integral protein.

scenes.tts: A second test uses sugars. Cells add N-linked sugars only inside the E R lumen. A sugar makes the protein run higher on a gel. If endoglycosidase H removes that shift, the end carrying the site reached the lumen. Sites closer than twelve to fourteen residues to the membrane go unused. So a missing sugar does not by itself prove the cytosol.

scenes.visual: Schematic. Inside the carried ER microsome, a branched sugar mark is added to a lumenal segment; the band on the schematic gel shifts up, then drops back when endoglycosidase H removes the sugar. A bracket marks a 12-to-14-residue zone next to the bilayer where a site receives no sugar even in the lumen, with a caution label 'No sugar ≠ cytosol'.

scenes.tts: These assays unlocked how cells insert proteins. In 1975, Günter Blobel and Bernhard Dobberstein applied protease protection to dog-pancreas microsomes. A mouse antibody light chain was trimmed and hidden inside, but only if membranes were present during synthesis. In 1981, Peter Walter and Blobel washed those membranes in high salt. Selective ribosome binding vanished until purified signal recognition particle restored it.

scenes.visual: Schematic two-part evolution of the carried microsome. First ('Blobel & Dobberstein 1975'): a growing mouse antibody chain threads into a dog-pancreas microsome during synthesis, loses its signal tip, and survives outside protease. Second ('Walter & Blobel 1981'): a high-salt wash strips a peripheral factor from the microsome so ribosomes no longer dock, then adding back purified signal recognition particle restores docking.

scenes.tts: In 1999, Goder, Bieri, and Spiess combined sugar mapping and alkaline extraction in C O S one cells. One added sugar site cut crossing by the chain's tail end, its C terminus, from about seventy-five to thirty percent. They concluded that growing chains can reorient inside the entry channel. Strip the surface, open the seal, and the parts reveal their sides.

scenes.visual: Schematic ('Goder, Bieri & Spiess 1999', COS-1 cells). In the carried microsome, a nascent chain reorients inside the membrane channel; an added lumenal sugar site is shown, and a schematic bar gauge drops C-terminal crossing from about 75% to 30%. The scene settles back on the full microsome showing surface wash, lumenal shielding, and detergent opening.
End card with the carried microsome faint behind large high-contrast text: 'Washes test burial; protease with and without detergent proves each side.'
